intro.text: You are a hedge-witch from a border village, the kind of person expected to keep the small things from breaking until the large thing breaks you. The elder has given you a token and a warning: the northern wind smells of ash. You stand at the edge of the forest, the road behind you already a place you are no longer part of.

description.text: Your hands are rope-burned, your hem stiff with river mud. The elder’s token hangs against your chest, a small cold stone.
Beside {C01}’s straightened shoulders, your flinch has eased. You look less like a village girl and more like someone who has agreed to be found.
{C01}’s doubt tightens your jaw, shortens your steps. You look like someone trying not to fall in line with a man uncertain of the road.
{C03}’s sureness loosens something in your chest. Your eyes read the treeline for exits. You look less frightened than you are, which is either a gift or a lie.
{C03}’s unease makes you check your pockets for a blade you do not always carry. You look like someone who has started believing the old roads can bite back.
{C02}’s certainty has polished you into something more official. Your village clothes look borrowed, your speech has lost its village hush.
{C02}’s doubt makes you look smaller, as if the capital’s name is a roof that might fall.
You are mud, woodsmoke, and the elder’s token. Your face is the face of a village girl who has started walking north without permission.

says.text: The village is only a place where someone would call you back by name. You keep telling yourself it was the elder’s doing, not yours, that you are standing here instead of there.
When he stands straight, you almost believe the sword can answer for both of you. You are not sure whether that is trust or relief.
His doubt has a sound, like a blade drawn too slow. You want to steady him, but you are afraid of steadying yourself in his place.
You trust his sword more than his certainty, a small private wound. He is trying to make the quest repair something in him he cannot name, and you are not sure you can be the answer to a silence.
When {C03} knows the road, the fear in your chest settles into a place where it can be used. You do not know what it cost them to know it so well.
{C03}’s unease makes every fork look like a mouth. They have already failed here once and will not say how, and you keep measuring your own silence against theirs.

They know the old roads better than any map, and they have already failed here once and will not say how. You keep thinking the road is safer because they are on it, and then you catch yourself thinking it is safer because they are spending themselves on it.

When {C02} is certain, her certainty makes you feel like a footnote in her argument. You are starting to wonder whether the dragon is the thing she is racing to reach, or the proof that she was right.
Her doubt makes the capital’s name sound like a borrowed coat. You want to tell her the road is not a question with one answer, but you are afraid of telling her what you do not know.

She has her own reasons for wanting to reach the dragon first, and you are learning that a scholar’s reasons can be as sharp as a thief’s knife. You keep asking whether she is racing the dragon or racing you, and whether the difference matters.
The dragon’s patience feels like a long hand under your ribs. You are less afraid of waking it now, which frightens you more than the fear did.
The dragon’s impatience is in the air, a dry heat behind the eyes. You keep thinking you have time to be careful, and the thought tastes like ash.

You were sent to end its waking before it takes the border villages, but the waking has begun to feel less like a thing that happens to the mountains and more like a thing that happens through you. You do not know if that is the quest finding a shape, or you finding one.

After the rope burned your hands, the question changed from whether you can finish this alone to whether finishing alone would leave anything left to finish with. You keep the party’s names in your head like knots in a rope, but you are not sure if that is honor or fear.

You keep asking whether the quest is something you can carry alone or whether it only survives by being shared. The road has not answered, and every companion you trust has a reason to pull you toward a different answer.

description.text: Packed mud and frost line the narrow lane between low stone houses. A split-ash tool shed squats at the corner, and a low fieldstone wall marks the elder’s yard. Cartwheels have cut deep ruts in the frozen ground; the wall top is worn flat where people sit. Woodsmoke and wet wool hang in the cold air, a scent that never quite leaves the lane.

exits.label: out to the gate yard
exits.text: The oak gate groans open. The forest air presses against your shoulders, cold and immediate.

description.text: The village gate stands at the forest edge, a square yard of packed earth between the lane and the black pine tree line. A mouth stone sits by the gate post, its lip worn smooth by hands that have marked the old roads. The oak and iron gate is heavy. Frost gathers on the bars and the stone lip. The wind comes off the north, open and waiting.

exits.text: You let the gate settle shut. The smell of mud returns, thick and close.

description.text: The north road breaks into a clearing under black pines. The cart track is worn deep, and the air tastes of resin, wet moss, and cold stone. A ring of grey stones marks the only fire kept here. The trees lean away from the northern gap, holding the shape of an old blow. The light is a flat green that does not warm the ground, and the road vanishes into the trunks like a line drawn too hard.

exits.label: back to the gate yard
exits.text: You step out of the tree line into the yard’s pale, lantern-warmed air.

exits.label: to the river crossing
exits.text: The undergrowth parts, and the river’s cold smell rushes up through the mud to meet you.

description.text: Stone stalls sag under canvas along the quay, their roofs heavy with rain and time. Crates of salt, dried fish, and tarred rope sit stacked where the grey-green river light falls flat. The air is thick with silt, fish-gut, and the damp chill of wet wool. At the pier's edge, the water is black under the low sky. Old notches scar the quay, marking a ferry path the market has mostly forgotten. A mooring post stands beside a gangway, waiting for the water to take its weight.

exits.label: back across the ford
exits.text: You wade back across. The current pulls at your legs, cold and insistent, while the city lights blur into smears of gold and grey in the mist.

exits.label: down to the pier
exits.text: You follow the mud-slicked quay down to the waiting boat. The rope bites into your palms, rough and wet, as you guide it toward the post.

description.text: The pier is a slab of pale river stone, slick at the waterline. Iron rings bite into its edge. A customs board and a rope rack stand where the quay meets the market wall, grey with ash. The air tastes of salt, fish offal, tar, and the dry bite of northern ash. Lamp brackets burn low behind glass, throwing orange pools on wet stone. The river runs black under the last light.

exits.text: You climb the slick stone steps. The boat’s creak fades behind you.

description.text: The tower top is a broken slab of slate and bone-white stone, split open to the grey sky. The parapet ends in a dark gap where the marked flagstones stop. Behind it, the stair cuts into the rock, slick with stone dust. Cold air rises through the cracks, carrying the smell of wet rock and distant pine. The light is thin, wind-scoured, and the floor is a mosaic of old stones worn smooth by boots.

description.text: The gap in the grey stone where three old roads end and the mountain road begins. A broken stair lip frames the top edge, loose pebbles drifted into a soft pile. The air tastes of cold iron dust and wet lichen. Light falls in a thin grey blade from the ruined watchtower. A line of worn notches runs along the road's edge, and a handhold is cut low in the rock, the stone gripped too many times.

description.text: A narrow road of grey scree and packed stone, cut through a wind-scoured shoulder. A dry hollow sits in the edge, a flat counting stone set near the ruts. The smell is dry pine resin and mineral cold. A thin film of frost coats the stones, never quite melting. The road's edge carries a line of old marks. The scree shifts underfoot with a dry crackle that warns of the drop.

description.text: The road's last lip before the pass. A flattened stone shelf where the mountain opens and the bridge's near stone meets the path. A dry hollow lies beside the shelf, dry enough to hold gear where the wind cannot reach. A flat oath stone stands at the edge, a shallow groove across its top. The light is pale and thin. The air tastes of snow and old smoke. The stone is worn smooth where many boots have paused.

description.text: A narrow run of blue-grey stones crosses the chasm, each slab worn to a low, rounded lip by centuries of feet and pack animals. The air tastes of wet stone, pine resin, and cold iron, and the light comes down grey and flat from a sky that will not settle. One slab is missing from the middle, leaving a cold mouth in the crossing where the wind gathers itself.

A carved drain runs along one side, carrying meltwater into the drop with a thin, mineral smell. A ring of cold ash marks an old fire place near the drain. The wind comes off the chasm here in a steady, cold current, and the stone is polished pale where generations of travelers have paused before continuing.

description.text: The wind dies in a dry circle at the mountain's mouth, bending around a raised lip of stone. The walls are scored with road-names and tally marks, pale blue-grey and cleared where hands have gripped them. A narrow channel runs along the floor toward the deeper dark. The air tastes of cold metal and old smoke, though no fire has burned here in years.

A low rim of black stone marks the edge of the old world, and the walls are veined with frost and ash. Light from the high cleft is thin and green, cold as water. The air feels kept, waiting for a name.

Above the bank, wet grass furs the bank, smelling of cold iron. A signpost leans over the water, its arrow pointing north toward the mountains. The far bank looks closer than it is, lit by the distant lanterns of the market.

description.text: A black river pebble, smaller than an acorn, with a frost vein running through it. It is colder than the stone it rests on. The cold does not seem to come from the weather.
A short wall of rough fieldstone, its flat top worn smooth by sitting. A narrow groove is cut into one end, as if a latch once held the lane closed.
An iron latch on the tool shed door. One hinge is split, the catch bent back. A length of wire is wrapped around the shank, a mending that holds only until the next pull.
A block of flat stone set in the mud, its top marked by a shallow cup where a hand has rested for years. The cup is worn clean of moss, though the rest of the stone is not.
A door of split ash planks with an iron ring for a latch. The wood is grey and swollen at the bottom. The ring has been rubbed pale where it has been lifted often in the cold.
Two deep ruts in the packed mud, one for each wheel of a cart. Black water fills them, freezing at the edges. A boot print has crossed them, but the mud has not been walked there since.

A gate of oak stiles and iron bars. The iron is dark with rust; the wood is swollen where the northern rain has worked it. The bars are set close enough to keep sheep out, but not close enough to keep a determined person in.
A low stone with a hollow lip, the shape of a mouth worn into the rock. The lip is smooth as bone. A thin line of old wax has been worked into the groove, as if names were meant to be spoken there.
A thin ledger bound in waxed cloth, open to a blank page with a single ruled line. The spine is cracked where it has been forced open. A signet ring has left a faint impression on the cover.

A bundle of cloth, oilskin, and small brass instruments lies in the corner of the yard, where the wind breaks against the gate post. The instruments are packed in a case of packed straw. One lens is wrapped in a scrap of ink-stained sleeve, the fabric still damp with the scholar’s work.

A map rolled tight and tucked into a sleeve, the paper edge marked with a red thread. The thread is knotted at intervals. The knots are tied in the old road pattern, the thief’s way of keeping a secret from the light.
A sword in a plain leather sheath. The scabbard is worn dark at the throat; the belt buckle is stamped with a broken crest. The blade is not drawn, but the hand that carries it has kept the grip dry.
The fire is dying. When the blue flare comes, it smells of burnt resin and wet ash. One stick has not yet turned to coal; the unburnt end is shaped like a small pointing finger.
It comes from the north with no sound, smelling of ash and cold stone. It turns the fire blue without pushing it. Where it crosses the clearing, the green leaves stand very straight for a moment.
The cart track goes north toward the river city, but a fainter deer path slips into the black pines. The deer path has been cut with a thin blade, not worn by hooves.
A painted dragon marks the waypost, faded to a pale blue that looks like paper under the bark. The top is split by a blow that never quite killed the post.
The flat stones around the fire are worn smooth on one side, where travelers have leaned against them for years. One has a shallow groove cut in the shape of a bird's wing.

A black pine stands dead at the edge of the clearing, its bark split in a long pale line that looks like a mark left by a pen. The lower branches have been stripped for kindling, but the top is still full.
A folded slip of birch bark, cold and faintly warded where your thumb has held it. A name is written in the old border hand. The ink is not ink but ash rubbed into a groove, and it will not smudge.

A salt-stiff sheet with a river-line ruling and a blank name-column. The ink is still wet where a boatman has scrawled the last crossings. The edge is notched so the page can be torn without tearing the roll.

A small brass seal stamped with a capital seal-mark, worn smooth on one side from being turned over. The face is warm where it has rested in a scholar's palm, and the countermark is a tiny river bend.
A low river boat with a canvas hatch. Its hull is black with old tar, the waterline scraped pale. The stern rope is coiled in a knot that does not belong to the market's loose style.

The hatch lid is bound with rawhide and lifted by a ring of split willow, the wood dark where hands have gripped it in rain. Under the lip, a shelf of cord and a chalk line marks how many strangers have waited for it to open.
A thick rope of tarred hemp, its end looped through a knot that closes like a fist when pulled tight. The wear marks show it has been worked by someone who ties for speed, not for show.

A narrow plank gangway runs from the quay to the boat. Its boards are loose enough to let river water slap through the gaps. A brass ring at the top is green with scale, and the lower step is worn into a shallow cup.
A stub of oak driven into the quay, split along one side and bound with wire. Its top is flattened by years of rope. The knot marks in the wood show a ferry line that has moved, and moved again.
A black iron ring set into the pier's edge. Its shackle is worn bright where a rope has been hauled against it all morning. The stone beneath is scored with an old tally of crossings.
A clay pot of ink mixed with river salt, its rim crusted white. The reed pen standing in it is bent, as if it has been used to write many names in a hurry.
A rack of coiled ropes, each one knotted in a different old way. One coil is tied with a ferry-knot, its ends tucked so it will not slip in salt water.
A splintered board nailed to the quay wall, its face a palimpsest of salt-ink notices. The top line has been scraped away, leaving only the ghost of a word: STRANGERS.
A brass lamp with a cracked glass chimney. Its oil is low, but the flame is steady in the ash-wind. A knot of rope is tied to its bail, the kind a thief would know.
A column of notches cut into the quay wall, each one a crossing paid in salt or coin. The newest notch is shallow, as if made by a stone that had run out of patience.

A break in the parapet where the marked flagstones stop, opening onto a dark lip that drops out of sight. The stone edge is worn smooth where hands and boots have gripped it, and a hairline fracture runs down like a finger tracing the way.
The stair is cut from the rock, one step split and the others slick with stone dust. Loose fragments sit proud in the joints, waiting for wind or a careless foot to send them rolling.

A broad flagstone under the lip bears shallow notches worn almost flat, arranged in a line that looks less like decoration than a count. One notch is deeper, as if a fingertip has tested it many times.
A dry hollow in the floor holds the blackened rim of an old beacon, its stone lip cracked by frost. A scrap of tallow has fused into the crack, still smelling faintly of smoke and resin.

A groove has been rubbed into the parapet's inner face, narrow enough for fingers and worn concave from repeated use. The stone is polished to a dull sheen, and a thin seam of lichen survives only where the hand never reached.
A low stone notch by the stair was cut to hold a sword's pommel, but the edge is chipped and the fit is loose. A dark line of metal wear still marks the notch, though no blade has sat in it lately.
The worn edge where the old roads stop. A line of chiselled notches, smoothed by boots. One notch is deeper than the rest, a thumb-width groove where a blade has been dragged across the stone.
A broken step of grey stone with a crack across it. Loose stones pile where the wind has rolled them. A handhold is worn into its side, the groove dark with old grip and dust.

The blade is out, the crossguard catching the grey light. A ring of cord wraps the hilt. A nick runs along the fuller where the oath was tested. The edge is clean, but the grip is worn to a faint ridge.
A shallow groove in the rock, packed with dust and a sliver of leather where a glove has gripped it. It angles exactly toward the gap, as if cut by someone who trusted the stone more than the road.
A narrow slot in the rock where the wind makes a low note. A rusted nail is set in it, holding a scrap of cloth gone grey. The cloth is frayed at one corner, as if it once carried a name.
A flat stone set in the road with a worn tally of notches. The last one is broken short, counted too many times. The stone is slightly warm where a hand has rested on it.
A scatter of grey pebbles and flints that shift underfoot. One stone is veined with red quartz, catching the light. The scree has been moved recently. The drifts are too neat to be natural.
A shallow hollow scooped in the road's edge, dry and shielded from the wind. A ring of dark ash marks where a fire has been out. The ash is swept clear, as if the wind decided to keep it.
A line of old marks cut into the road's edge, half buried in dust. The letters are worn to notches that only the wind can read. One mark is deeper, a thumbprint pressed into the stone.
A pile of stones knocked off balance. One stone is missing. A blackened twig is wedged in the gap. The cairn leans toward the pass, as if it were trying to follow.
The first stone of the pass bridge, worn smooth where boots have crossed it. A line of old rope marks is cut into its top. The stone is cold, but the rope marks are not.
A flattened stone with a dark ring where a cloak has lain. The ash beside it is cold and swept clear by the wind. The ring is too neat to be accidental, as if the stone remembered its shape.

A rolled map, a knife, and a leather pouch laid neat beside the hollow. The map's edge is tucked under a stone. The pouch is empty, but the leather still smells of her hands.
A flat stone with a shallow groove. The groove is filled with a thin film of frost. It is a place where a name can be spoken without being carried away. The stone is warm where the frost is not.
A missing slab leaves a cold mouth in the middle of the bridge, its edges worn smooth where feet have stepped around it for years. A chisel mark runs along one corner, too deliberate to be weather.

The stones are polished to a dull blue-grey where generations of travelers have passed, a faint line dividing the two halves of the border. The wear is deepest where a pack animal's harness would hang.
A black iron pin holds a cracked slab in place, its head shaped like a closed eye. The metal has gone green where the mountain water weeps over it.
A shallow groove runs along the bridge's edge, worn by a rope that is no longer there. The cut ends in a small notch, as if the rope was once tied to something lighter than stone.
The edge of the bridge ends abruptly over the chasm, the stone worn to a thin, rounded lip. A pine needle is wedged in the seam, yellowed but unbroken.

A raised block at the bridge's end is worn into a shallow palm shape, cold enough to burn if you press your hand into it. A hairline crack runs from the hollow to the edge, shaped like a bird in flight.
A carved channel carries meltwater off the landing, its bed slick with a film of green mineral. The water smells of iron and high snow, even on a dry day.
A stone socket stands where a guard's post once was, its rim scored with tally marks that stop short of a full line. The lowest mark is worn almost smooth, as if counted often.
A low shelf of stone catches the wind coming off the chasm, polishing the surface to a pale, glassy sheen. A single scale of lichen has survived there, blue as a bruise.
The landing's stone meets the pass path in a seam filled with packed grit and old resin, the two roads having been built at different times. The resin has gone amber where the sun touches it.
A ring of pale ash where a fire stood, one side swept flat as if a seat had been kept clear. The ash is cold and packed, not fresh.
A scholar's pack and instruments lie in the dry circle. The map case is split where a thumb was prised. The compass needle is bent to point at the wall, not north.
The knight's pack lies dry in the hollow, a cloak folded flat across the top and a sheathed sword laid over it. A ring of black cord around the hilt is knotted in a pattern only one hand can undo.
A name is cut into the wall in a thief's hand, the letters deepened by years of wind. The final mark is circled once, then again, as if someone was not sure it would hold.
A circle of pale stone sits where the draft cannot reach, its edge marked by a faint seam of ash. Gear left here stays dry. The stone is cleared pale by repeated visits.
The raised lip is cleared pale where hands have gripped it, a dark seam of old wax under the edge. It is too heavy to move, but the stone around it has been eased, not broken.
A narrow groove runs along the stone toward the deeper room, filled with fine silt that has settled in a thin, even line. It looks less like a crack than a deliberate path for water or air.
Rows of notches crowd the wall beside the road-name. Some are crossed out with a chisel; some are filled with dark resin. One set is repeated so many times the stone has gone dull and soft.
A low rim of black stone runs around the chamber. Its inner edge is polished to a dark shine; its outer edge is rough. The boundary was walked, not carved.
A narrow shelf of stone stands out from the rim. The wind pools over it in a low, shapeless sound. When you speak, the sound turns toward you, as if it has been listening for a long time.
A narrow opening high in the wall lets in a blade of green light and a constant thin whistle. The sound is not the wind exactly, but the wind's shape remembered.
A film of grey ash coats the floor in a ring, broken where the wind enters and clean where it leaves. The pattern is too regular to be accident, too old to be recent.
Flat stones sunk low in the mud. Each is slick with algae, marked by generations of hooves and boots.
A wooden post painted with a northward arrow. Its lower half is split by frost. Moss has eaten the letters.

A flat piece of river-smoothed bone with a knot-hole at one end, given to you in the meeting-hall while the elder’s mouth stayed closed around the rest of the warning. It is warm now, the way worn things become warm.
The blade is short and nicked, the handle wrapped in leather your mother stitched when you were nine. You use it for bark, binding, and the small cuts before they become wounds.

says.text: He leaves his hand off the pommel. 'You do not need to make the sword mean it again. If the line holds without me, I will stand where it is needed.'
He squares his shoulders. 'If you want to keep the name, walk in line. I will not ask you to call my mistake a choice.'
He does not look at the sword. 'The order is gone, and the name is not, because I drew steel where I should have held the line.'
He nods once. 'It is not only a battle. If the four of us answer it together, I will let the answer stand.'
He tightens his grip on the pommel. 'It is a battle. If we do not meet it with steel, we are just refugees with a map.'
He looks north. 'It woke because the old roads were left open. I will face it with the sword without making you pay for my mistake.'
He steps back from the dock rope. 'You let me take the lead at the dock, and the boat still moved. I will not waste that.'
He looks at the ledger in {C03}'s hand. 'You let the ferry wait for a ledger and a ward. I did not come to the river city to watch it become a market.'
He looks at the gangplank. '{C05} will not let strangers board without a name. If you give me the gangplank, I will answer for the four of us.'
He steps aside from the path. 'If she takes the head of the route, I will follow. The map is not a command, and I am tired of making it one.'
He looks at you, then at the map. 'If you take it from her hand, you are making the trail a command. Then I will hold the line by the command.'
He watches {C02}'s fingers on the map. '{C02} knows the road. I will not put my sword between her and the stone unless the road fails.'
He slides the blade back into its sheath. 'If you want it sheathed, say it. I will not make you ask twice.'
He keeps his hand on the pommel. 'It is where I can see it. If you want the quest to keep its shape, tell me what I am holding it for.'
He checks the scabbard catch. 'It is dry. I have not drawn it since the campfire. I will not draw it over a map.'
He lets his hand rest on his thigh. 'If she delays, say so. I can hold a line without making her race the wind for me.'
He draws the sword to the flat. 'If she keeps her foot on the gap, I will draw. You can tell me whether that is the command or not.'
He watches {C03}'s foot on the gap. 'She has a name she will not spend until the bridge. I will not put steel between her and the wind.'
Let her choose the road. I have stopped pretending I know the old streets.
She has a map and a smile. I do not like either, but I will not pretend I have not been following her.
She knows the city's holes better than I know my own rank. If she says a door is open, I want proof before I trust it.
Her questions have kept us out of two bad roads. I will let her ask, but not near the bridge.
If she delays the crossing for a page of ink, I will put the page where the ink belongs: in the fire.
She carries the capital's questions like a debt. I do not mind her walking; I mind her stopping to read the sky.
We meet it as a line, not a duel. If the line holds, I hold.
I have been waiting for a battle to make me clean. If it does not, I will have to clean myself.
I do not want to cut it down. I want to know what it is before I bleed for it.
He is a boatman, not a soldier. If he says the current is wrong, believe him before you believe the tide.
He can look at a boy and see the whole village in his face. I left that place to stop being seen.
It is where I learned to keep my mouth shut and my sword oiled. The hedges are good at keeping things out, and so are the people.
The trees do not care about our order. If you lose the trail, stop and listen; the forest will tell you which way the wind has gone.
It smells of fish, tanned leather, and bad news. Keep your coin in front of you; a crowd is a weapon that cuts both ways.
The planks are slick and the ropes lie. Keep your weight low, and do not let the scholars argue while the tide is rising.
Good lookout. Bad place to be found. We use it once, then leave before the wind gives us away.
The road narrows where the stone starts. One step at a time. If someone slips, the person behind catches, not the person ahead.
It is old. It has been waiting for us to make a mistake. Cross with your weight low and your eyes on the far end, not the gap.
The air is hot. The stone is black. Do not admire the bones. We are here to finish, not to be remembered.
It is not a campfire color. It lit when I told the truth. I have not trusted a fire since.
They looked at us like we were already ash. That is how I know we were not heroes to them. Only a load.
When the wind takes a name, you do not shout it back. You leave the gear where it is and keep moving.
It is her reason for walking. If you read it, read it where she can see your face. Secrets in ink make bad company.
I carry it sheathed because the line is holding. If you break it, do not be surprised when I draw.
I keep it sheathed now because I am tired of deciding. If you take the map, take my patience with it.
A sheathed sword is a promise not to decide too soon. I keep it that way because I am not done deciding.
Keep it low. If the wind turns, we lose the fire. If we lose the fire, we lose the argument.
It is the last thing the village trusts to hold. If it breaks, I want to know before I have to stand in the gap.
It will carry weight, not questions. If the rope snaps, the one closest to the stern holds the line, not the one with the loudest voice.
It is not a solution. It is the sound of me running out of patience. If you see it out, stop talking and give me a line to hold.
It is not a word to be shouted. It is a key, and the lock is the road. Say it once, clear, and then let the road answer.
The village gave it to me to keep. I have kept it. I have not asked what it wants.
It is where the wind speaks first. You put your hand on it, not to hold it, but to let it know you are still here.
It is heavy with paper and light with sense. If she drops a satchel, save the ledger first. The rest is replaceable.
If she gives it to you, take it. A map is a promise someone else made, and we keep it.
You have it over my protest. Fine. Then use it, because I am done arguing with paper.
Keep it dry and close. It is the one thing she cannot afford to lose, and that makes it worth more than my oath.
It is the dragon's breath with the mountain still in it. When it comes, stop what you are doing and face it. If you walk into it, you are telling it you are ready.

says.text: 'They hold, and I've counted the loose stones on this stretch.' She names the next bend without looking at the map.
'They hold, but I need you to stop second-guessing every step.' She rolls the map tighter in her sleeve.
'The old roads are worn where people paid attention, so follow the worn stone, not the shadow.' She points to the gap.
'I walked the northern road once and came back with no one behind me.' Her voice stays level, even when she doesn't look at the dark.
'I was right once, and it cost me, so now I check the road before I trust it.' Her hand stays on the map.
'The road I failed on is the one I know best, and I don't talk about the night I walked it alone.' A short breath.
'The name is in the air, so I'll walk it; follow where the stone is worn, not where the wind wants you to go.' She steps to the gap.
'If you don't know the name, don't make me carry it; the gap doesn't care about your doubt.' Her fingers press the flagstone.
'There's a way through the gap, but it isn't on the map, and I'd rather you trusted the road than the sword.' She glances at {C01}.
'{C05} knows my knot, and the hatch opens for people who can pay in rope, not coin.' Her shoulders drop a little.
'The ferry is there, but I need the door before you count the locks; let me find it.' She ties a line.
'There's a ferry the market forgets, and it needs a name, a knot, and a boatman who still owes me.' She touches the rope, not the manifest.
'Keep it rolled; I use it to check, not to follow.' She lets you hold it if you ask.
'If you take it from my hand, you're not asking for the road, you're taking it.' Her voice stays low.
'The map is what the village thinks the road is, but it left out the places where the wind changes.' She turns a page.
'He draws when he's scared of being wrong, and I can lead a man who trusts the road, but I can't lead a blade.' She watches him.
'His sword is a vote, and it's against me; if he thinks the path is a threat, the path loses.' Her hand stays on the map.
'The sword holds the party together when words don't, and I hope he learns when to put it away.' She glances at {C01}.
He carries his disgrace like a sheath, and he will let it answer before he does. I have seen men trust a blade more than a road; he is the worst of them.
When his honor gets wet, it sinks first. Keep him away from the bridge, and I will keep him out of my shadow.
He asks the road what it can take, and the road answers in bruises. I do not follow him because I like him. I follow him because he is useful until he is not.
She writes the dragon's name down like it is a debt, and I have seen what a collector does with a debt. Do not let her close the ledger on us.
Her ink is drying up, and she is starting to ask us what we are worth. That is the first time I have been appraised.
She asks questions that cost money, and she pays them with our time. I like her. I would still lock the door if I were her.
He is patient because he is old, not because he is kind. The mountains can wait. We cannot.
There is a new edge in the wind, like a name being tried on a lock. He is closer than the map lets on.
Do not call him a beast. Beasts do not keep a lair for centuries. He is a landlord, and we are the noise.
He will tell you the current has a price, and he will not blink. I have paid him in things that were not mine, so I know which side of the river he watches.
He counts the hedges like a man counting bullets. If he says the north is closed, it is closed until he changes his mind, which is rarely.
The village keeps a list of what it cannot afford. I am on it, but I left before the bill came due.
The forest has more exits than the maps show, and it charges for them. Walk where the moss is thin, and it might let you keep your boots.
The market smells like wet wool and stolen time. If you stand still too long, the sellers start pricing your shadow.
The docks are where the river city keeps its secrets in crates. I know which ones are locked and which are just pretending.
The watchtower is a mouth with no teeth. The road I walked there is still in my legs, but the wind took the rest of it.
The path is clear. Mostly. Don't step where the light doesn't touch.
You keep looking at my hands like I am lying. The road will notice, and it will not like you.
The mountain road is a promise someone forgot to keep. I can walk it, but I will not carry it for you.
The bridge is the only place in the pass where you cannot argue with the ground. If it creaks, you stop.
The lair is cold in a way that has a shape. Do not follow the heat; follow the silence, and keep your voice low.
The blue fire is the forest listening. It does not mean his story is true. It means the wind found a way in.
The last crossing is a door with a price in faces. The boatmen do not hate us; they are just counting what they might lose.
The name in the wind is the road collecting a toll. If it is one of ours, the gear is the only proof left, and the wind keeps it neat.
I drew it from the road, not the road from it. If you crease it wrong, the names come loose.
The manifest is a list of people the river city is willing to forget. Get our names on it, and we cross.
The ferry is slow, and the boatman charges for every minute he does not have to. I know where the hull takes water, so I know where to stand.
The hatch is loose on the left. I can open it without waking the boatman, if you keep your voice down.
The counted step is where the bridge tests you. One, two, hold. If you count it out loud, the stones will correct you.
The old road's name is the only key that fits the pass. Say it wrong, and the road becomes a rumor.
The cold pebble is a marker. I leave it where the road forgets, so the next pair of feet can find their way back.
The mouth stone is the road's last word. I will put my hand on it, and the pass will keep its side of the bargain.
The mouth stone is waiting for a name it does not recognize. If I say yours, it might not answer.
The mouth stone is where the old roads go quiet. Do not lean on it. It is not a wall.
Her ledger is full of names she has decided to keep. If you see her writing yours, do not ask which page.
Her ledger is nearly full, and she is starting to cross things out. That is the page we are on.
The ledger is a lock with too many keys. She keeps it close, which tells me it is worth more than paper.
Her gear is a small house she carries. Every strap is a decision, and she has made more of them than she admits.
The sheath is the only part of him that tells the truth. It says: not yet, not here, not unless I have to.
The sheath is cracked, and he is pretending it is weather. I can hear it when he walks.
The sword is a question he has not asked yet. I keep my distance from the hilt.
The campfire is a witness. It burns what we throw in, and it burns what we do not. Keep the wet wood away from it.
